thesis: UPDATE to the open LULU long (opened 2026-08-22 at 115.00, now 99.72, -13.3%). The turnaround thesis is finished on the company own numbers. On 2026-09-03 lululemon cut FY2026 guidance for the third time this year — revenue to $10.35-10.50B from $11.0-11.15B and EPS to $9.48-9.73 from $10.95-11.15 — and guided Q3 revenue to $2.29-2.32B, a 10-11% year-over-year DECLINE against a $2.53B consensus. The Q2 EPS beat of $2.92 versus $1.82 was not operational: 86 cents came from tariff refunds and interest, leaving roughly $2.06, on revenue that fell 4% to $2.4B and missed. A business whose revenue is shrinking double digits while guidance is cut three times in one year is not a de-rated compounder, it is a broken one.
key_risk: Selling at an eight-year low into an incoming-CEO transition is exactly when a kitchen-sink reset bottoms. Heidi O Neill takes over with the bar on the floor, and the first post-transition print is the squeeze risk.
counter_argument: The strongest bull case is that the third cut IS the capitulation and the new CEO now owns clean numbers. Answered by the shape rather than the level: a 10-11% revenue decline guided for the current quarter is demand, not accounting, and no CEO reverses a demand decline within one quarter. If the turnaround is real it can be re-bought later on evidence, at a price, rather than held through it at a 13% loss.

thesis: Qualcomm has been de-rated to 15.5x trailing earnings (about $11.36 TTM EPS against a 176.40 close) on one problem — a handset-royalty base concentrated in a customer that is insourcing its modem — and on 2026-09-03 it signed an agreement that addresses exactly that problem. Per the 8-K filed 2026-09-08, Qualcomm issued Amazon a warrant for up to 25,000,000 shares at $161.26, vesting in tranches tied to the execution of commercial arrangements, the placement of binding purchase orders and actual purchases of QTI server chip products, technology, systems and manufacturing services, up to a maximum of $60 billion in payments. Against roughly $40B of annual company revenue, a $60B multi-year ceiling on server silicon is not an incremental product line, it is a second franchise, and it is in AI inference and 1.6T optical connectivity rather than training, which is the part of the datacenter build that scales with usage instead of with capex budgets.
key_risk: The $60 billion is a maximum warrant-vesting threshold, not an order book, and the timeline is undisclosed — revenue could be years out and arrive far smaller. **Explicit invalidation, which is not a price move:** two consecutive quarterly reports with no disclosed server/datacenter revenue line, or an 8-K reporting forfeiture or expiry of unvested warrant tranches. Either means the ramp is not converting and the thesis is wrong regardless of where the stock trades.
counter_argument: The strongest case against is that this is a press-release partnership — and notably the 2026-09-08 press release itself contains no financial terms, no purchase commitment and no timeline, so anyone reading only the release is right to be sceptical. The 8-K answers it: 3,750,000 shares were vested on issuance based on initial purchase commitments, and the remainder vests on binding purchase orders and actual purchases. Amazon has taken a position that pays only above $161.26 and only if it actually buys. That is capital and commitment at risk, not an announcement.

thesis: Crude is at $97.19 after a 4.47% day, its highest since May, on physical Middle East supply loss, and the energy complex has repriced everything except services. Refiners are done paying: VLO closed 0.06% off its 120-day high after +81% off the low, MPC 0.64% off after +89.6%, DINO 1.57% off after +95.1%, and XLE itself is 0.9% off its high. Halliburton is still 14.8% below its own 43.59 high while trading above both its SMA20 35.51 and SMA50 34.20. Services revenue follows the oil price with a lag because operators commit capital to activity only after a price move persists, so the laggard here is a sequencing artefact rather than a judgement on the business — and the sequencing has started to turn.
key_risk: This is a macro-driven long with no company catalyst, in the one energy sub-sector that needs the oil price to STAY high rather than merely to spike — a ceasefire headline reverses the thesis without touching a single Halliburton fundamental. The sell-side is also already crowded on the long side at 76.5% bullish (26 of 34 at buy or strong buy), and insiders sold $17.7M over six months with zero open-market purchases, so neither positioning nor management is confirming.
counter_argument: The strongest case against is that $97 crude is a war premium and premiums decay: sign a ceasefire and services gives back a month of gains in a session. Answered by what actually moved the price — this is physical, not positioning. Houthi attacks forced an actual temporary suspension of some Saudi energy operations, Middle East exports are constrained with production shut-ins in the region, and China is restocking dwindling inventories. Shut-in production and drawn-down inventories take quarters to restore, not a headline, and rebuilding them is itself services demand. The premium can deflate while the activity thesis stays intact — which is why the stop sits below the SMA50 rather than under the last few days of noise.

thesis: The commodity is at a 10-month high and the equities that mine it are priced as if it were not. Uranium spot reached $89.65/lb on 2026-09-08, up 3.28% over the month and 16.81% year-over-year, with analysts modelling $85-95/lb through 2026 and spikes above $100. Against that, URA closed 20.5% below its own 120-day high, and the divergence is uniform across the group rather than a single broken constituent — UEC is 31.1% off its high, LEU 22.8%, NLR 18.3%, CCJ 23.5%. Uranium equities are a delayed claim on contracted fuel prices, and the contracting cycle is where a spot move at a 10-month high actually gets paid, so the gap between a rising commodity and a de-rated equity complex is the trade. URA closed above both its SMA20 45.74 and SMA50 43.18, so the tape has already stopped going down.
key_risk: This overlaps the open CCJ long, which is the same driver — size the pair together, not each on its own, because two positions on one uranium view is one position with extra steps. The target of 58.97 is 25.8% away, which is the upper bound of a swing horizon and roughly seven ATRs; it needs a trend, not a bounce, and the scale plan exists because of that. Uranium equities also trade with far more beta than the metal, so a spot retrace to the mid-$70s takes URA back toward its 37.18 low much faster than the rally brought it here.
counter_argument: The strongest case against is that the divergence is information rather than opportunity: the equities de-rated 20-31% while spot rose, which is the market saying miners will not capture the spot price because utility contracts are struck years in advance at lower fixed prices, and because AI-datacenter nuclear demand is a 2030s story being paid for today. That is a real risk to the timing and is why this is a conviction 3 at 2% rather than a core position. What answers it partially is policy that has already moved money — a $2.7B DOE enrichment commitment and an $80B reactor-construction term sheet are appropriated and signed, not forecast.

evidence.detail: URA 46.86 closed above SMA20 45.74 and SMA50 43.18, 20.5% below the 120-day high of 58.97 and 26.0% above the 37.18 low. Target 58.97 IS that prior high; the 42.80 stop sits below the SMA50, giving 4.06 of risk on a 1.73 ATR = 2.35 ATR, clear of the 1.8 ATR ETF floor.

Relative strength of the commodity against its own equities, measured: uranium spot $89.65/lb on 2026-09-08 (+3.28% 1m, +16.81% y/y, a 10-month high) while URA sits -20.5% off its high, UEC -31.1%, LEU -22.8%, NLR -18.3% and CCJ -23.5%. The whole complex lags the metal, so this is a sector-wide de-rating and not one broken holding.
